entries.question: What was Solomon's gift to Hiram?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 5:11 says Solomon gave Hiram 20,000 measures of wheat and 20 measures of pure oil annually for his household. 2 Chronicles 2:10 says Solomon gave 20,000 measures of wheat, 20,000 measures of barley, 20,000 baths of wine, and 20,000 baths of oil to the timber workers. The commodities, quantities, and recipients differ.
entries.commentary:
Three differences in one parallel: the commodities (oil-only versus oil-wine-barley-wheat), the quantities of oil (20 measures versus 20,000 baths), and the recipients (Hiram's household versus the timber workers).

The harmonization commonly offered is that these are two separate payments: 1 Kings 5:11 describes Solomon's annual payment to Hiram personally for his household, while 2 Chronicles 2:10 describes a separate payment to the Tyrian and Israelite workmen cutting cedar in Lebanon. Two transactions, two beneficiary groups. That actually works better than most of the harmonizations in this batch. The Hebrew of 2 Chronicles 2:10 explicitly addresses the hewers, the timber-cutters, and not Hiram personally. The Hebrew of 1 Kings 5:11 explicitly addresses Hiram's household. So the recipient distinction is genuinely in the text.

What doesn't reconcile so cleanly is the oil quantity in the Hiram-household payment. 1 Kings 5:11 says "twenty measures of pure oil." Twenty cors of beaten oil is a small amount — manageable as an annual household allowance, even for a king. The Septuagint of 1 Kings 5:25 actually reads "twenty thousand," agreeing with Chronicles, which suggests the MT of Kings may have a textual error, dropping the second part of the number. If we accept the LXX reading, the Hiram-household payment becomes 20,000 cors of wheat plus 20,000 cors of oil, matching the scale of the workmen's payment in 2 Chronicles 2:10.

That reconstruction makes the contradiction smaller but doesn't eliminate it. Even with the LXX emendation, 1 Kings 5 still doesn't mention wine or barley, while 2 Chronicles 2 includes both. So either the Kings author is selectively listing only some commodities, or the Chronicler is expanding the list. Both are common practices in their respective authors. The cleanest reading: two payments, with MT Kings possibly suffering a number-corruption on the oil, and Chronicles preserving a more complete commodity list for the workmen payment.

entries.question: How many overseers did Solomon have?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 5:16 reports that Solomon employed 3,300 overseers over the temple workforce, while 2 Chronicles 2:18 puts the number at 3,600. The two passages describe the same administrative tier of the same building project and produce a flat numerical discrepancy of 300.
entries.commentary:
The plain reading is brutally simple. 1 Kings 5:16 (MT 5:30) says 3,300 chief officers ran the labor force. 2 Chronicles 2:18 (MT 2:17) says 3,600. Same king, same temple, same job category — different number. The Chronicler is working from a source that is essentially the Kings text and is changing it.

Apologists like Gleason Archer in the *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties* try to rescue the count by claiming Kings and Chronicles are counting different supervisory tiers — that Kings excludes 300 Israelite foremen who Chronicles includes, or vice versa. The problem is that 1 Kings 5:16 and 2 Chronicles 2:18 use parallel descriptions of the same group ("those who ruled over the people that did the work"), and the harmonization requires inventing a sub-category nowhere named in either text. That is the apologist playbook, page one — postulate an unstated category whose only purpose is to absorb the numerical gap.

Critical scholarship treats this as one of dozens of small numerical drifts between the Deuteronomistic History and the Chronicler. Sara Japhet in her *I & II Chronicles* (OTL, 1993) and Steven McKenzie in the *Abingdon Old Testament Commentaries* volume on 1-2 Chronicles (2004) both note that the Chronicler systematically reshapes Solomonic numbers, often inflating them or rounding them to fit theological purposes — here likely combining the 3,300 chiefs of 1 Kings 5:16 with the 250 chief officers of 1 Kings 9:23 into a tidy 3,600 (Japhet, p. 549). It is a transmission/redaction problem, not a hidden harmony.

Verdict: this is a textbook scribal/redactional discrepancy. The harmonization works only if you invent an extra category of overseers that neither text mentions. The more parsimonious reading is that the Chronicler adjusted the figure.

entries.question: When did Solomon's reign begin?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 6:1 places Solomon's fourth regnal year — when temple construction begins — 480 years after the Exodus. Paul's speech in Acts 13:17-22, combined with the regnal data from 1 Chronicles 29:26-27, produces a total of roughly 570+ years between the Exodus and Solomon's accession, contradicting the Kings figure by about 90 years.
entries.commentary:
1 Kings 6:1 gives a precise schematic number: 480 years from the Exodus to Solomon's fourth year. Subtract the four years and you get 476 years from Exodus to accession. That is the Deuteronomistic chronology, period.

Paul in Acts 13:17-22 walks through a different chronology — 40 years in the wilderness, conquest, judges for "about 450 years," then Saul for 40 years, then David. 1 Chronicles 29:27 confirms David's 40-year reign. Add it up: 40 + an unspecified-but-real conquest period + 450 + 40 + 40 = around 570 years before you even get to Solomon's accession. The numbers don't reconcile to the 1 Kings 6:1 figure no matter how you slice it.

Apologists handle this in two main ways. The first is to argue that "about 450 years" in Acts 13:20 refers to the cumulative period from the patriarchs *through* the judges, not just the judges era — a reading promoted by F.F. Bruce in his NICNT volume on Acts. The second, championed by Eugene Merrill in *Kingdom of Priests*, is to claim 1 Kings 6:1's "480" is a symbolic 12×40 generational schema, not a literal year count. Both moves concede the obvious — that a straightforward reading produces a contradiction — and then dissolve one number into vagueness to save the other. That is post-hoc rationalization, not harmonization.

Critical scholars from Martin Noth onward treat 1 Kings 6:1 as a Deuteronomistic theological schema (12 generations of 40 years) rather than a historical datum, which is the more honest concession. Either way, Acts 13 and 1 Kings 6:1 cannot both be literally accurate chronologies of the same span. Take your pick: literal 480 from Kings and demote Paul's math, or literal Acts chronology and demote Kings as schematic.

entries.question: Which tribe was Hyram from?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 7:13-14 says Hiram, Solomon's master craftsman, was the son of a widow from the tribe of Naphtali. 2 Chronicles 2:13-14 says his mother was from the tribe of Dan. The two texts identify the same craftsman's maternal lineage as belonging to two different Israelite tribes.
entries.commentary:
1 Kings 7:14 is unambiguous — Hiram's mother is "a widow's son of the tribe of Naphtali." 2 Chronicles 2:14 is equally unambiguous — "the son of a woman of the daughters of Dan." Same person, same job, different tribal affiliation.

The standard harmonization, going back to Keil-Delitzsch and reproduced by Archer, is that Hiram's mother was originally a Danite who married a Naphtalite, was widowed, and was "reckoned" as Naphtalite by marriage. That requires assuming a double-tribal identity nowhere stated in either text and treating Chronicles' "daughters of Dan" as a maiden-tribe descriptor and Kings' "of the tribe of Naphtali" as a married-tribe descriptor — neither passage cues that distinction. It's a fix that only exists because the contradiction needs fixing.

Critical scholars are more straightforward. Sara Japhet (*I & II Chronicles*, OTL) and Ralph Klein (*2 Chronicles*, Hermeneia) both treat the Chronicler's change as deliberate — possibly to associate Hiram with Bezalel's tribal partner Oholiab from Dan in Exodus 31:6 and 35:34, drawing a typological link between the wilderness tabernacle's craftsman and the temple's craftsman. Steven McKenzie notes the same pattern in his AOTC volume. That's a theological move, not a confused historical memory.

The "both tribes" harmonization isn't impossible, but it requires extra-textual assumptions the texts themselves don't support. The more parsimonious reading is that the Chronicler is reshaping the tradition for theological resonance with Exodus.

entries.question: How high were the pillars?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 7:15 (paralleled by 2 Kings 25:17 and Jeremiah 52:21) gives the bronze pillars Jachin and Boaz a height of 18 cubits each. 2 Chronicles 3:15 reports them as 35 cubits high. The Chronicler's figure nearly doubles the Kings figure for the same two pillars.
entries.commentary:
Three independent witnesses in the Hebrew Bible — 1 Kings 7:15, 2 Kings 25:17, and Jeremiah 52:21 — give the pillars a height of 18 cubits each. The Chronicler stands alone at 35 cubits. The numerical drift is not subtle.

The most popular harmonization, advanced by Keil-Delitzsch and repeated by Archer, says 2 Chronicles 3:15 reports the *combined* height of both pillars (18 + 18 = 36, close enough to 35 with rounding or a one-cubit base shared between them). The problem is that 2 Chronicles 3:15 explicitly says "two pillars of thirty-five cubits high" — the number is attached to each pillar, not to a sum. To get the harmonization to work, you have to re-translate the Hebrew against its plain grammatical sense. Japhet (OTL) and Klein (Hermeneia) both reject this reading on syntactic grounds.

A second harmonization claims the difference reflects different points of measurement — base included vs. excluded, or shaft vs. shaft-plus-capital. This collides with 1 Kings 7:16, which gives the capitals as an additional 5 cubits each on top of the 18-cubit pillar height, meaning Kings is already distinguishing capital from shaft. There's no room to absorb a 17-cubit gap into capital-measurement quibbles.

The critical reading is that the Chronicler is working with a corrupted or theologically inflated figure. Klein points out the LXX of 2 Chronicles 3:15 reads thirty-five for the combined or individual measurement depending on manuscript, suggesting early scribes recognized the problem and tried to fix it. The simplest explanation is textual corruption or deliberate inflation. Either way, the harmonization requires fighting the Hebrew.

entries.question: What was the volume of the molten sea in Solomon's temple?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 7:26 states the molten sea held 2,000 baths. 2 Chronicles 4:5 says it held 3,000. The two passages describe the same single vessel in the same temple and disagree on its capacity by 50 percent.
entries.commentary:
Same vessel. Same temple. Same author tradition. 1 Kings 7:26 says 2,000 baths. 2 Chronicles 4:5 says 3,000 baths. The Chronicler is working with the Kings text and changing the number.

The standard apologetic move, again from Archer, is that Kings reports the normal working capacity while Chronicles reports the maximum capacity if filled to the brim. That distinction is not in either text. Both passages use the same Hebrew root for "contained" / "received and held" (kûl). Inventing a working-vs-maximum distinction to absorb the gap is the same template move used for every Chronicles-Kings number discrepancy — postulate an unstated category.

A second harmonization tries to fix it geometrically. The bath measure may have changed over time, or the cubit used in Kings differs from the cubit used in Chronicles. The problem is that neither text signals different units, and the dimensions of the sea (1 Kings 7:23 // 2 Chronicles 4:2) are identical: ten cubits across, five deep, thirty around. Same dimensions can't yield different volumes unless the units changed mid-paragraph, which the texts don't say.

Critical scholarship treats this as one more instance of the Chronicler inflating Solomonic numbers. Japhet (OTL, pp. 565-566) and Klein (Hermeneia 2 Chronicles, pp. 64-65) both note the systematic pattern of inflation across the Chronicler's account of the temple. Cogan (AB 10) calculates that the geometry given in both texts produces a volume closer to the Kings figure than the Chronicler's. The parsimonious reading is that the Chronicler is making the temple bigger, holier, and richer than its source presents it.

entries.question: Does God dwell in darkness or in light?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 8:12 and 2 Chronicles 6:1 declare that Yahweh said he would dwell in thick darkness, with Psalms 18:11 and 97:2 echoing the imagery. 1 Timothy 6:15-16 says God dwells in unapproachable light. The same deity is given mutually exclusive habitats by different biblical authors.
entries.commentary:
The Solomonic dedication speech in 1 Kings 8:12 has Yahweh choosing thick darkness — *araphel* — as his dwelling place. The same word recurs in Psalm 18:11 and 97:2 and runs through the Sinai tradition in Exodus 20:21 and Deuteronomy 4:11. This is the ancient Near Eastern storm-god imagery: Yahweh enthroned on dark cloud, hidden by smoke, inaccessible by darkness.

The Pastorals flip the metaphor completely. 1 Timothy 6:16 describes God as the one "dwelling in unapproachable light, whom no one has seen or can see." The inaccessibility is preserved, but the medium of inaccessibility has inverted from darkness to light.

Apologists like Walter Kaiser in *Hard Sayings of the Bible* try to dissolve this by claiming "darkness" and "light" both function as metaphors for divine hiddenness — God is unapproachable, and whether that's expressed as too-dark or too-bright is just figurative variation. That reading isn't crazy, but it concedes the literal contradiction in favor of treating both as metaphor. The deeper issue critical scholars raise is that the *theology* of the two metaphors is different. Mark Smith in *The Origins of Biblical Monotheism* shows that the *araphel* tradition is part of Yahweh's identity as a storm/mountain deity assimilated from older Canaanite imagery, while the light theology of the Pastorals is filtered through Hellenistic-Jewish abstraction (Wisdom of Solomon 7:26, Philo).

The contradiction is real if you take the texts literally, dissolved if you take both as metaphor — but in dissolving it, you also concede that biblical descriptions of God's dwelling are culturally conditioned rather than literally informative. That is of course a subjective call on how to read theological poetry, but it is the more parsimonious reading of the evidence.

entries.question: Does God dwell in temples?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 8:13 and 2 Chronicles 7:12, 16 declare that God's name and presence will dwell in the Jerusalem temple Solomon built. Acts 7:48 (Stephen's speech) and Acts 17:24 (Paul at the Areopagus) flatly deny that the Most High dwells in temples made with hands. The same deity is depicted as both occupying a specific building and refusing to occupy any building.
entries.commentary:
The Solomonic dedication speech in 1 Kings 8 is one long meditation on Yahweh choosing to dwell in this particular building. Verse 13 has Solomon saying, "I have surely built thee a house to dwell in." 2 Chronicles 7:16 has Yahweh himself confirming, "I have chosen and sanctified this house, that my name may be there forever." That's about as explicit as ancient temple theology gets.

The NT speeches push the opposite direction. Stephen in Acts 7:48 quotes Isaiah 66:1-2 to argue "the Most High dwelleth not in temples made with hands" — and the rhetorical context is an indictment of Jerusalem temple worship as misplaced. Paul at the Areopagus in Acts 17:24 makes the same point against Athenian temples, but with the same universal scope: God does not dwell in shrines built by humans.

Apologists handle this with the "transcendence vs. immanence" move. Solomon himself, in 1 Kings 8:27, asks rhetorically "will God indeed dwell on the earth? Behold, the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee, how much less this house?" So, the argument goes, the Hebrew Bible already acknowledges God transcends the temple, and the NT speeches are just emphasizing that transcendence over against pagan or rote temple religion. That harmonization works at the level of broad theology — both testaments hold both ideas in some tension. But it doesn't dissolve the specific verbal contradiction: the temple texts say God's name *does* dwell there, the Acts speeches say the Most High *does not* dwell in such houses. The harmonization just chooses which verses to treat as literal and which as rhetorical.

Critical scholarship treats the development as historical theology. The Deuteronomistic "name theology" of 1 Kings 8 (God's *name* dwells in the temple while God himself dwells in heaven) is already an attempt to mediate the tension. By the time of Stephen's speech, that name theology has been pushed further by post-70 CE Jewish-Christian polemic into outright rejection of temple-based dwelling. Richard Pervo in his Hermeneia *Acts* and Ben Witherington in *The Acts of the Apostles* both read Acts 7:48 and 17:24 as a deliberate appropriation of Hellenistic-Jewish anti-idolatry rhetoric. The texts are doing different theological work in different eras.

entries.question: Is anyone without sin?
entries.books_in_tension: 1 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Romans, 1 John, 3 John
entries.summary: 1 Kings 8:46, 2 Chronicles 6:36, Proverbs 20:9, Ecclesiastes 7:20, Romans 3:23, and 1 John 1:8-10 all declare that no human is without sin. 1 John 3:6, 3:9, and 5:18 declare that anyone born of God does not sin and cannot sin. The Johannine epistles internally affirm both that all sin and that the regenerate do not sin.
entries.commentary:
This one is fun because the contradiction is internal to a single short letter. 1 John 1:8 says, "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us." Two chapters later, 1 John 3:9 says, "Whosoever is born of God doth not commit sin... and he cannot sin, because he is born of God." And 5:18 doubles down: "Whosoever is born of God sinneth not." Same author, same letter, opposite claims about whether Christians sin.

The standard harmonization is the Greek-tense move. 1 John 3:6 and 3:9 use the present-tense Greek *hamartanei* and *poiei hamartian*, which apologists like I. Howard Marshall (NICNT) and Daniel Akin (NAC) argue should be read as durative or habitual — "does not habitually sin" — while 1:8-10 refers to occasional sins that the regenerate still commit. That gives you "the Christian sins occasionally but does not live in sin habitually."

The problem is twofold. First, the durative-present reading of *hamartanei* is grammatically possible but not required, and many Greek scholars including Stephen Smalley in his WBC volume reject it as importing a distinction the Greek tense doesn't carry on its own. Second, even if the durative reading is granted, 1 John 5:18 reads "*we know* that whosoever is born of God *sinneth not*" — a flat assertion that pushes back against the "all have sinned" frame of Romans 3:23 and 1 John 1:8.

Critical scholars like Raymond Brown (Anchor Bible 30) and Judith Lieu (NTL) treat this not as a grammatical puzzle but as a literary one — 1 John is responding to a secessionist group who claimed sinless perfection (1:8-10 rebukes their claim), but the author also wants to insist that genuine regeneration produces real ethical change (3:6-9, 5:18). The author holds both in tension because the polemical situation requires both. That's not a harmony — that's an unresolved tension in the text itself, dressed up later by readers who want it to be consistent.

Verdict: the harmonization works only if you import a tense-distinction the Greek doesn't always carry, and even then 1 John 5:18 still slaps. The more parsimonious reading is that 1 John is fighting on two fronts and the result is internally inconsistent.

entries.question: How many officers did Solomon have?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 9:23 reports that 550 chief officers oversaw Solomon's construction projects. 2 Chronicles 8:10 puts the number at 250. The same administrative tier, in the same king's reign, gets two different totals from the two parallel histories.
entries.commentary:
1 Kings 9:23 says 550 chief officers. 2 Chronicles 8:10 says 250. A 300-officer gap.

The rabbinic and apologetic harmonization, repeated by Archer in *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties*, is the same one used for the 3,300 vs 3,600 overseer count in entry 261: combine the two numbers in different ways to balance out. The argument goes that Kings counts only Israelite officers (550) and Chronicles counts only non-Israelite officers (250), or vice versa, with the two totaling 800. The problem — same problem as in entry 261 — is that neither text signals an ethnic subdivision of the officer corps in this verse. The harmonization invents the subdivision to make the math work, and the supposed combined total (800) appears nowhere in either book.

A related move points out that earlier in the same chapters, 1 Kings 5:16 has 3,300 chief officers and 2 Chronicles 2:18 has 3,600. So if you add 1 Kings 5:16 (3,300) + 1 Kings 9:23 (550) = 3,850, and 2 Chronicles 2:18 (3,600) + 2 Chronicles 8:10 (250) = 3,850, you get matching grand totals. That's a real arithmetic coincidence, and it's the cleanest harmonization available. But it requires assuming the Chronicler is partitioning the same total differently from Kings — that is, deliberately changing the numbers in both verses to preserve the sum — which is itself an admission that the two texts disagree at the verse level. The grand total may match by design, but the individual verses still contradict.

Critical scholars including Japhet (OTL) and Klein (Hermeneia 2 Chronicles) acknowledge the arithmetic coincidence but treat the verse-level discrepancy as evidence of the Chronicler's editorial reshaping rather than a real harmony. Either way, the cleaner reading is that the numbers don't match at the verse level, and the apologetic "add them up across passages" move concedes the point while pretending to resolve it.

entries.question: How many talents of gold did Hiram send Solomon?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 9:27-28 says Hiram's fleet brought 420 talents of gold from Ophir. 2 Chronicles 8:18 puts the figure at 450 talents. The two texts describe the same voyage, the same king, and the same gold shipment, with a 30-talent discrepancy.
entries.commentary:
Same expedition. Same Phoenician fleet. Same destination (Ophir). 1 Kings 9:28 says 420 talents. 2 Chronicles 8:18 says 450. Thirty talents of gold off — at the standard talent weight of roughly 75 pounds, that's over a ton of bullion.

Apologists have basically three options. The first, from Archer, is textual corruption: somewhere in transmission, a Hebrew numeral letter got copied wrong. This is actually the most honest harmonization, because it concedes that the texts as we have them disagree and locates the problem in scribal copying rather than in the original autographs. It also doesn't try to invent semantic categories that aren't there. The downside, for the apologist, is that admitting scribal corruption admits that the text we have is not numerically inerrant.

The second move, used in Keil-Delitzsch and J.A. Thompson's NAC 9 *1, 2 Chronicles*, is that the 30-talent gap represents shipping costs, royal commission, or some other deducted amount. Same template as every other Chronicles-Kings numerical entry — invent an unstated category to absorb the gap.

The third, less common move, is to argue Kings reports net delivered and Chronicles reports gross before loss at sea or other depletion. Same template, different label.

Critical scholars treat this with the same parsimony as the other Chronicler discrepancies. Japhet (OTL) notes that 30 is a common scribal-error candidate in Hebrew numeral letter confusion, and Klein (Hermeneia) concurs. The simplest explanation is either scribal slip or the Chronicler's habit of inflating Solomonic wealth. Take your pick — but each option concedes the texts as transmitted disagree.

entries.question: Is God the creator of evil?
entries.books_in_tension: 1 Kings, 2 Kings, Job, Psalms, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Amos, 1 John
entries.summary: Isaiah 45:7, Lamentations 3:38, Amos 3:6, and a stack of prophetic passages including Jeremiah 4:6, 18:11 and 2 Kings 6:33 explicitly attribute the creation or bringing of evil to Yahweh. Psalm 5:4 says God has no pleasure in wickedness and evil does not dwell with him; 1 John 4:8 says God is love. The Hebrew Bible's prophetic frame and the moral attributes ascribed to God in later texts pull in opposite directions.
entries.commentary:
Isaiah 45:7 is the clearest case: "I form the light, and create darkness: I make peace, and create evil [*ra'*]: I the LORD do all these things." Amos 3:6 follows: "Shall there be evil in a city, and the LORD hath not done it?" These are not isolated verses; they sit inside a coherent prophetic theology where Yahweh is the sovereign source of both blessing and calamity.

The apologetic move pivots on Hebrew lexicography. The word translated "evil" in the KJV — *ra'* — has a semantic range that includes "calamity, disaster, misfortune" as well as "moral evil." Apologists like John Oswalt in his NICOT *Isaiah 40-66* and Walter Kaiser in *Hard Sayings* argue that Isaiah 45:7 is about Yahweh causing physical calamity, not moral evil, and Psalm 5:4 / 1 John 4:8 are about moral character. So no contradiction — God brings calamity but does not commit moral wickedness.

That reading isn't wrong about the Hebrew. *Ra'* genuinely covers both senses, and the Isaiah 45:7 context (cosmic creation, light/dark, peace/calamity) does favor the calamity sense. So at the level of word-study, the apologist has a real point. But the harmonization has a deeper problem: the prophetic texts repeatedly attribute morally weighted actions to Yahweh — destroying cities, killing children, sending lying spirits (1 Kings 22:23). The 1 John 4:8 "God is love" framework and the Psalm 5:4 "evil shall not dwell with thee" framework simply cannot absorb the prophetic Yahweh's behavior without redefining "love" and "evil" to mean whatever Yahweh happens to do. That's a circular escape, not a harmony.

Critical scholarship treats this as theodicy development across the canon. Jon Levenson in *Creation and the Persistence of Evil* shows the Hebrew Bible's older strata are comfortable attributing calamity to Yahweh because the moral-evil/created-evil distinction hadn't yet been worked out. Later Second Temple and NT theology pushed the responsibility for moral evil onto Satan, demons, or human free will to protect God's moral character — but that pushes the texts of Isaiah and Amos out of step with the texts of John. The contradiction is at the level of theological frameworks across different periods, not just word definitions. That is of course a subjective call on what "evil" means, but the prophetic texts say what they say.

entries.question: How did Jeroboam die?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 14:20 says Jeroboam I "slept with his fathers" — the standard Deuteronomistic idiom for peaceful death. 2 Chronicles 13:20 says the LORD struck him and he died, after he failed to recover strength following his defeat by Abijah. The two texts give incompatible accounts of the same king's manner of death.
entries.commentary:
1 Kings 14:20 uses the formula *wayyishkav 'im 'avotav* — "he slept with his fathers" — and reports a 22-year reign followed by his son Nadab succeeding him. The phrase is the Deuteronomistic Historian's standard idiom for a king dying of natural causes, contrasted with violent deaths that get explicitly narrated (e.g., Nadab killed by Baasha, Elah killed by Zimri).

2 Chronicles 13:20 reads completely differently: "Neither did Jeroboam recover strength again in the days of Abijah: and the LORD struck him, and he died." Same king, same general period, but now his death is a direct divine punishment following military defeat. The verb *nagaph* ("struck") is the same verb used elsewhere of Yahweh smiting Egyptians, Philistines, and other condemned figures.

The standard harmonization, from Archer and Keil-Delitzsch, says "the LORD struck him" and "he slept with his fathers" can both be true — God afflicted him with a wasting illness, he lingered, and he eventually died in bed. Some apologists also note that 2 Chronicles 13:20 says he didn't recover "in the days of Abijah," which could imply he lingered into Asa's reign. So the harmony would be: divine smiting → wasting → peaceful eventual death.

The problem is that the Chronicler's whole rhetorical point in 2 Chronicles 13 is theological retribution — Jeroboam led Israel into idolatry, Abijah defeated him in battle (2 Chronicles 13:15-19), and the LORD struck him dead as part of that judgment. The Chronicler is not describing a long, peaceful illness; he's narrating divine punishment-by-death. The harmonization works only by treating the Chronicler's theological reading as compatible with the Deuteronomist's silence, when the Chronicler is clearly *correcting* or *supplementing* the Deuteronomist with a theology of retribution.

Critical scholars like Japhet, Klein, and Dillard and the broader Chronicler-focused literature treat this as a standard pattern: the Chronicler systematically theologizes royal deaths to fit a strict reward/punishment scheme that the Deuteronomistic History often leaves ambiguous. The texts disagree at the level of theological framing, not just narrative detail.

entries.question: Who was Abijam's mother?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 15:2 names Abijam's mother as Maachah, daughter of Abishalom. 2 Chronicles 13:2 names her Michaiah, daughter of Uriel. The same king's mother is given two different names and two different fathers.
entries.commentary:
1 Kings 15:2 — "his mother's name was Maachah, the daughter of Abishalom." 2 Chronicles 13:2 — "his mother's name also was Michaiah the daughter of Uriel." Different name. Different father. Same king.

Apologists work three angles. First, the name-variation move: Maachah and Michaiah may be two forms of the same name, or one of them is a nickname. The Hebrew forms *Ma'akah* and *Mikhayahu* are not phonologically related and have different theophoric structures — *Mikhayahu* contains the divine name Yah, *Ma'akah* does not. This is not a spelling variant. So the name-variant harmonization is weak.

Second, the family-genealogy move from Keil-Delitzsch and Archer: Maachah is identified in 2 Chronicles 11:20-22 as Rehoboam's wife and the daughter of Absalom (i.e., David's son). The proposal is that Maachah was actually the *granddaughter* of Absalom through his daughter Tamar, who married Uriel of Gibeah. So her father was Uriel, her grandfather was Abishalom (= Absalom), and she went by two names — Maachah (matching her grandmother Maacah, Absalom's mother per 2 Samuel 3:3) and Michaiah. This is a real attempt to reconcile the genealogies, and it does have some textual support in Josephus, *Antiquities* 8.249-250, which reads Tamar as the daughter of Absalom who married Uriel.

But the harmonization stacks multiple unstated assumptions: that Maachah went by two unrelated names, that "daughter of Abishalom" really means "granddaughter," and that an otherwise unattested marriage between Tamar and Uriel is the missing link. Critical scholars including Japhet (OTL, pp. 690-691) note that "daughter of" can sometimes mean "granddaughter" in Hebrew genealogies, but the more direct reading is that the Chronicler is working with a slightly different tradition or correcting Kings.

McKenzie in his AOTC volume on Chronicles notes that the Chronicler frequently adjusts genealogical and onomastic details from Kings, and the Maachah/Michaiah variation is likely one more instance. Verdict: the harmonization is possible but requires several silent assumptions to land. The texts as written disagree.

entries.question: How were Abijam and Asa related?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 15:8 says Asa was Abijam's son, succeeding him on the throne. 1 Kings 15:1-2 gives Abijam's mother as Maachah daughter of Abishalom; 1 Kings 15:9-10 gives Asa's mother as Maachah daughter of Abishalom — implying the two kings share the same mother and are therefore brothers, not father and son.
entries.commentary:
1 Kings 15:8 says, "Abijam slept with his fathers... and Asa his son reigned in his stead." Plain succession from father to son. But back up two verses to 1 Kings 15:2 and you find Abijam's mother is "Maachah, the daughter of Abishalom." Then jump down to 1 Kings 15:10, and Asa's mother is "Maachah, the daughter of Abishalom." Same name, same patronymic. So either Abijam and Asa are brothers (same mother, same maternal grandfather, contradicting v. 8 that says Asa is Abijam's son), or there's a problem.

Apologists handle this with the "mother" / "queen mother" / "grandmother" distinction. The Hebrew *'em* can be used loosely for an authoritative female figure, including a grandmother in the role of *gebirah* (queen mother). Since 1 Kings 15:13 has Asa removing Maachah from the position of *gebirah* — which is the formal queen-mother title — the harmonization claims that Maachah was Abijam's actual mother and Asa's grandmother who retained the queen-mother role into his reign. So 1 Kings 15:10 calls her Asa's "mother" in the queen-mother sense, not the biological sense.

This is one of the more defensible harmonizations in the Chronicles/Kings series, because there's a real institutional category (queen mother / *gebirah*) that explains the dual usage, and 1 Kings 15:13 explicitly identifies Maachah as the figure being deposed from that role. Mordechai Cogan in his AB 10 *I Kings* (pp. 397-398) and Niels-Erik Andreasen's CBQ article on the queen mother both support this reading.

But the harmonization has a softer underside. The text of 1 Kings 15:10 reads simply "his mother's name was Maachah, the daughter of Abishalom" with no signal that it means "grandmother in queen-mother capacity." Same wording as 1 Kings 15:2 for Abijam. If you didn't already know about the queen-mother institution, you'd read this as a flat contradiction. The harmony requires the reader to import the institutional category from v. 13 and apply it back to v. 10.

Verdict: this is a contradiction at the verbal-surface level that can be defused if you grant the *gebirah* reading, which is well-attested. But the texts as written give matching mother-statements for both kings, and that ambiguity is real. Slightly weaker contradiction than the rest of the Chronicles/Kings entries, but coherent enough to keep on the list.

entries.question: Did Asa remove the high places?
entries.summary: 2 Chronicles 14:3-5 says Asa took away the high places out of all the cities of Judah. 1 Kings 15:14 and 2 Chronicles 15:17 say the high places were not removed during Asa's reign, even though his heart was perfect with the LORD. The same king's same religious reform is reported as both accomplished and not accomplished — with the contradiction sitting inside Chronicles itself.
entries.commentary:
This one is sharper than the typical Chronicles/Kings discrepancy because 2 Chronicles contradicts itself. 2 Chronicles 14:3 (MT 14:2) says Asa "took away the altars of the strange gods, and the high places." 2 Chronicles 15:17 says "the high places were not taken away out of Israel." Same king, same book, opposite verdict — separated by one chapter.

1 Kings 15:14 agrees with the second Chronicles passage: "the high places were not removed." So the conflict isn't just Kings vs. Chronicles; it's internal to Chronicles, with Kings backing one of the two Chronicles statements against the other.

The standard apologetic resolution distinguishes between *bamot* dedicated to foreign gods (removed by Asa per 2 Chronicles 14:3) and *bamot* dedicated to Yahweh outside the Jerusalem temple (not removed). Hebrew Bible scholarship recognizes both categories existed — see, for example, the high place at Gibeon where Solomon offered sacrifice to Yahweh in 1 Kings 3:4. So the distinction is real, and Dillard's WBC volume and Selman's TOTC argue this is the correct reading. Asa removed the foreign-cult high places but tolerated the Yahweh-cult high places that the Deuteronomist views as illegitimate.

The problem with this harmonization is that 2 Chronicles 14:3 doesn't restrict its claim to foreign-cult sites. The verse says Asa "took away the altars of the strange gods, AND the high places" — two coordinate objects of "took away," with no implication that "the high places" is limited to foreign-cult sites. The text reads as a comprehensive religious purge. To restrict it to foreign-cult sites, you have to import the limitation from outside the verse.

Critical scholars like Japhet (OTL, pp. 706-710) treat this as the Chronicler's editorial inconsistency: the source-text (Kings) said Asa did NOT remove the high places, but the Chronicler's theology of retribution requires that righteous kings be rewarded with success. So the Chronicler adds 2 Chronicles 14:3-5 to give Asa a religious-reform credit before settling Asa's record into the original Kings frame later. The verses contradict because the Chronicler is welding a theological correction onto an inherited source.

entries.question: When did Baasha die?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 16:6-8 says Baasha died and his son Elah began to reign in the 26th year of Asa, putting Baasha's death no later than Asa's 26th year. 2 Chronicles 16:1 says Baasha came up against Judah and fortified Ramah in the 36th year of Asa — ten years after his death according to Kings. The Chronicler places a living, militarily active Baasha a decade after Kings says he was already dead.
entries.commentary:
The chronology in Kings is internally tight. Baasha reigned 24 years (1 Kings 15:33) starting in Asa's 3rd year, putting his death in Asa's 26th-27th year. 1 Kings 16:8 confirms Elah his son began to reign in Asa's 26th year. So Baasha is dead by Asa's 26th year, full stop.

Then 2 Chronicles 16:1 drops the bomb: "In the six and thirtieth year of the reign of Asa, Baasha king of Israel came up against Judah, and built Ramah." Ten years after Kings says Baasha was dead and buried, Chronicles has him leading military campaigns.

The apologetic standard response, going back to Keil-Delitzsch and championed by Edwin Thiele in *The Mysterious Numbers of the Hebrew Kings*, is that 2 Chronicles 16:1's "36th year of Asa" is not really year 36 of Asa's personal reign but year 36 of the *divided kingdom* (counting from the schism after Solomon's death). Under that interpretation, the divided-kingdom 36th year corresponds to Asa's actual 16th year, and Baasha is still alive. Thiele's scheme is the most popular resolution and has been adopted by Dillard (WBC 15, pp. 122-126) and Selman (TOTC).

Thiele's reading has two real problems. First, it requires a counting convention that the Chronicler does not signal anywhere in the text — "36th year of Asa" is the natural reading, and importing a divided-kingdom dating system to fix the contradiction is the textbook ad-hoc move. Second, Japhet (OTL, pp. 731-735) notes that the Chronicler everywhere else dates by individual royal years, never by divided-kingdom era; making this one verse the exception is special pleading. Third, even if you grant Thiele's scheme, you've conceded that the text as written produces a contradiction and needs an external chronological key to dissolve it.

The critical reading, advanced by Klein (Hermeneia), is that the Chronicler is reorganizing the sequence of Asa's reign to fit the theological scheme where Asa's earlier piety (chapters 14-15) is rewarded with peace and his later faithlessness (chapter 16) is punished with war. The chronological dislocation is theological framing, not a coded reference to divided-kingdom dating. Take your pick: Thiele's hidden calendar trick, or the Chronicler reshaping the chronology for theology. Either way, the surface reading is a contradiction.

entries.question: Was Jehu the son or grandson of Nimshi?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 19:16 calls Jehu the son of Nimshi. 2 Kings 9:2 (and 9:14) calls him the son of Jehoshaphat son of Nimshi, making him Nimshi's grandson. The same person is given two different relationships to the same ancestor within the same narrative complex.
entries.commentary:
1 Kings 19:16: "Jehu the son of Nimshi shalt thou anoint to be king." 2 Kings 9:2: "Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi." The simplest reading: one verse skips a generation.

The apologetic move, used by Archer and standard in Keil-Delitzsch, is that in Hebrew genealogy "son of" can mean "descendant of" — most famously in Matthew 1:1 where Jesus is called "the son of David, the son of Abraham" even though he is not literally David's or Abraham's son. So 1 Kings 19:16 just uses the looser sense, naming Jehu's more famous ancestor (Nimshi) without listing the immediate father (Jehoshaphat). This is a real lexical possibility — *ben* in Hebrew does have a wider range than English "son."

Mordechai Cogan and Hayim Tadmor in their AB 11 *II Kings* (pp. 107-108) accept this as the simplest reading and treat the dual usage as a non-issue: 1 Kings 19:16 names the prominent patronymic, 2 Kings 9 spells out the full lineage. The contradiction dissolves at the lexical level if you grant the standard Hebrew sense of *ben*.

The weakness of this harmonization, raised by some critical scholars, is that 2 Kings 9 itself uses both formulas — Jehu is called "son of Jehoshaphat son of Nimshi" in 9:2 and 9:14, but "son of Nimshi" in 9:20. So the narrator alternates between the two forms within the same chapter. The harmonization that *ben* means "descendant of" works fine, but it concedes the texts are using imprecise language, which is the same kind of imprecision that elsewhere produces real chronological and genealogical headaches.

Verdict: this is one of the weaker SAB contradictions in the batch. The Hebrew lexical range really does cover the gap. But it's still worth listing because the imprecise use of *ben* is itself a feature of biblical historiography that produces actual contradictions in other passages (Matthean genealogy, anyone?). I'd lean toward keeping it on the list while flagging that the harmonization here is more solid than for the numerical entries. That is of course a subjective call on which contradictions count as real.

entries.question: Did Elisha receive Elijah's mantle before or after Elijah is taken up into heaven?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 19:19 says Elijah cast his mantle on Elisha at their first meeting, before any departure. 2 Kings 2:11-13 says Elisha picked up the mantle that fell from Elijah only after Elijah was taken up by the whirlwind. The text describes two distinct mantle-transfers, with the second framed as if the first had not happened.
entries.commentary:
1 Kings 19:19 narrates Elijah's calling of Elisha at the plow: "Elijah passed by him, and cast his mantle upon him." This is the prophetic call-by-mantle, and the next verse has Elisha following Elijah and ministering to him.

2 Kings 2:11-13 narrates Elijah's ascension: "there appeared a chariot of fire, and horses of fire... and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven. And Elisha saw it... He took up also the mantle of Elijah that fell from him." Elisha picks up the mantle as a new, fresh transfer of prophetic authority.

This is actually one of the better SAB-listed contradictions because the harmonization is straightforward but exposes something interesting about the narrative. The standard apologetic resolution, used by everyone from Keil-Delitzsch to Wiseman in his TOTC, is that the 1 Kings 19 mantle-casting is the *initial call* (analogous to ordination), while the 2 Kings 2 mantle-falling is the *transfer of authority* at the master's death. Two separate ritual moments, two distinct functions of the mantle, no contradiction.

That reading works narratively and matches the way prophetic succession is depicted elsewhere in the ancient Near East. Marvin Sweeney's OTL volume on Kings and Volkmar Fritz's Continental Commentary both endorse it. The mantle in 1 Kings 19 marks Elisha as Elijah's *disciple*; the mantle in 2 Kings 2 marks Elisha as Elijah's *successor*. Different ritual moments.

Where the contradiction lives, on a stricter reading, is that 2 Kings 2 narrates the falling mantle as if Elisha didn't already possess one from Elijah. Elijah is wearing the mantle on his way up; it falls; Elisha picks it up. If Elisha had received a mantle a decade earlier in 1 Kings 19, then either (a) he gave it back, (b) Elijah had two mantles, or (c) the 1 Kings 19 mantle-casting was symbolic and the 2 Kings 2 transfer is the real article. Option (c) is what the apologist defends, and it is the most natural reading. The contradiction is real only if you press the 1 Kings 19 mantle-transfer as a literal handoff of the same garment.

Verdict: weaker contradiction than the numerical ones. The ritual-symbolic distinction handles it cleanly. Worth listing because it shows the doubled-tradition pattern in the Elijah-Elisha cycle, but I would not lead a debate with this one. That is of course a subjective call on which contradictions are debate-strength.

entries.question: Did God bring evil upon Ahab?
entries.summary: 1 Kings 21:27-29 has Yahweh promising that because Ahab humbled himself, the threatened evil would not come in his days but in his son's. 1 Kings 20:42 has the prophet telling Ahab that because he released Ben-Hadad, his own life would be forfeit. The two passages within ten chapters of each other depict God both sparing Ahab and condemning him to die for his sin.
entries.commentary:
This is one where the apparent contradiction has a real chronological-narrative answer, but the answer itself exposes something interesting about the redaction of 1 Kings.

1 Kings 20:42 is a prophetic oracle pronounced after Ahab releases Ben-Hadad of Aram: "thy life shall go for his life." Ahab is condemned to die for sparing the enemy king Yahweh had marked for destruction.

1 Kings 21:27-29 comes after the Naboth's-vineyard episode, where Ahab's repentance prompts Yahweh to defer judgment: "I will not bring the evil in his days: but in his son's days will I bring the evil upon his house."

The standard harmonization, used by Wiseman and Walsh and basically every commentator who reads Kings as a sequential narrative, says these refer to two different judgments. 1 Kings 20:42 is about Ahab's personal death (which does occur in 1 Kings 22:34-37 at Ramoth-Gilead). 1 Kings 21:29 is about the broader destruction of Ahab's *house*, which is what gets deferred to Joram's reign and ultimately accomplished by Jehu in 2 Kings 9-10. So one oracle targets Ahab personally, the other targets his dynasty. No contradiction.

This reading is correct as far as it goes. Ahab does die in battle (fulfilling 20:42), and his dynasty is wiped out a generation later (fulfilling 21:29). The narrative arc works.

Where it gets interesting is that critical scholarship — Marvin Sweeney's OTL, Volkmar Fritz's Continental Commentary, and Antony Campbell's *Of Prophets and Kings* — reads 1 Kings 20 and 21 as deriving from different prophetic source traditions that the Deuteronomistic Historian welded together imperfectly. 1 Kings 20 belongs to a pro-Ahab military narrative tradition where Ahab is mostly favorable, while 1 Kings 21 belongs to the Elijah cycle where Ahab is the archetypal apostate. The two source traditions had different verdicts on Ahab, and the redactor stitched them together with the 20:42 / 21:29 distinction that the apologetic reading then ratifies.

Verdict: the surface contradiction can be resolved by the personal-death/dynastic-fall distinction. But that resolution itself reveals the seams between different prophetic source traditions that the Deuteronomist combined. This one is on the weaker end of the SAB list as a strict contradiction, but it points to a genuinely important compositional issue. I'd flag it as resolved at the surface narrative level while noting the source-critical issue underneath.
